Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p\in M$. A **derivation at $p$** is an $\mathbb R$-linear map $v:C_p^\infty(M)\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$ v([f][g])=f(p)\,v([g])+g(p)\,v([f]) $$
for all smooth germs $[f],[g]\in C_p^\infty(M)$. The set of all derivations at $p$ is written $T_pM$ and called the **tangent space of $M$ at $p$**.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $M$, $N$, $P$ be smooth manifolds.

1. The identity map $\mathrm{id}_M:M\to M$ is smooth.
2. If $F:M\to N$ and $G:N\to P$ are smooth, then $G\circ F:M\to P$ is smooth.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

derivations.claim: Fix $v\in V$ and a smooth germ $[f]$ at $p$. By [L6] the curve $c(t):=p+tv$ has coordinate representation $x(c(t))=x(p)+tu$ with $u=E^{-1}(v)$, a smooth curve in $\mathbb R^4$; hence $c$ is a smooth curve through $p$ in the chart $x$, and $t\mapsto f(c(t))$ is smooth near $0$ by [L2], so its derivative at $0$ exists. If $g$ agrees with $f$ near $p$, then $f\circ c$ and $g\circ c$ agree near $0$, so the derivative depends only on the germ $[f]$; hence $\Phi_p(v)([f])$ is a well-defined real number.

With $u=E^{-1}(v)=(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$, set $F:=f\circ x^{-1}$, the smooth coordinate representative of $[f]$ near $x(p)$ [L2]. Then $f(c(t))=F(x(p)+tu)$ for $t$ near $0$, so by the chain rule [L4] applied to $t\mapsto x(p)+tu$ and to $F$, whose total derivative at $x(p)$ has matrix the Jacobian by [L3], $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigr|_0F\bigl(x(p)+tu\bigr)=D F(x(p))\cdot u=\sum_{a=0}^3u^a\partial_aF(x(p))$.
$\Phi_p$ is linear in $v$: by step 2.1 the value $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_au^a\partial_aF(x(p))$ is a linear function of $u=E^{-1}(v)$, and $E^{-1}$ is linear by [L6].

$\Phi_p(v)$ is a derivation at $p$: it is $\mathbb R$-linear in the germ because the sum and scalar-multiple derivative rules of [L7] apply to $t\mapsto f(p+tv)$ near $0$. For smooth germs $[f],[g]$, the coordinate representatives satisfy $((fg)\circ x^{-1})=(f\circ x^{-1})(g\circ x^{-1})$, so the one-variable product rule [L7] applied to the differentiable functions $t\mapsto F(y+t\mathbf e_a)$ and $t\mapsto G(y+t\mathbf e_a)$, where $y=x(p)\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\mathbf e_a\in\mathbb R^4$ is the $a$-th standard coordinate vector gives the product rule for the partial derivatives: $\partial_a((fg)\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=f(p)\partial_a(g\circ x^{-1})(x(p))+g(p)\partial_a(f\circ x^{-1})(x(p))$, since $f(x^{-1}(x(p)))=f(p)$ and likewise for $g$; substituting into step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f][g])=f(p)\Phi_p(v)([g])+g(p)\Phi_p(v)([f])$, so $\Phi_p(v)\in T_pA$ by [L1].

$\Phi_p$ is injective: suppose $\Phi_p(v)=0$ with coordinate vector $u=E^{-1}(v)$. Applying $\Phi_p(v)$ to the germ of the coordinate function $x^a$ gives, by step 2.1, $\Phi_p(v)([x^a])=\sum_bu^b\partial_b(x^a\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=\sum_bu^b\delta^a_b=u^a$; hence $u=0$, and since $E^{-1}$ is injective by [L6], $v=0$.

$\Phi_p$ carries the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ to the coordinate derivations: for $v=e_a$ one has $u=E^{-1}(e_a)=(\delta^a_b)_b$ by [L6], so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(e_a)([f])=\partial_aF(x(p))=\partial_a|_p([f])$ for every smooth germ, that is, $\Phi_p(e_a)=\partial_a|_p$. By [L5] the derivations $\partial_a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pA$, so the linear map $\Phi_p$ carries a basis of $V$ to a basis of $T_pA$; hence $\Phi_p$ is surjective (its image contains a basis) and injective by step 3.3, so it is a linear isomorphism $V\to T_pA$.

Finally, let $v=\sum_av^ae_a$; then $u=E^{-1}(v)=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_av^a\partial_aF(x(p))$, that is, $\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$. The construction uses only the affine structure $p+tv$ and the smooth structure of the model, both fixed independently of any choice of chart, so the isomorphism $\Phi_p$ is canonical.

Throughout, $c>0$ and $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with displacement space
$V$; $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and $x:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau:I\to J$ and inverse $\rho:J\to I$
([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]). By that
lemma $\tau$ is $C^1$ with

$$\tau'(s)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0 \qquad (s\in I),$$

$\tau$ is strictly increasing, $J=\tau[I]$ is an interval with at least two
elements, and $\rho:J\to I$ is $C^1$ with $\rho'(\tau(s))=1/\tau'(s)>0$ for
every $s\in I$.

**(a) The proper-time derivative.** Let $P:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ map, its
derivative $P'$ being the derivative of a $V$-valued function of one real
variable, read componentwise in any ordered basis of $V$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The **proper-time
derivative of $P$** is the map $\dot P:I\to V$ defined by

$$\dot P(s):=\frac{P'(s)}{\tau'(s)} .$$

This is well defined because $\tau'(s)>0$ for every $s\in I$, so the scalar
division by $\tau'(s)$ is a legitimate vector-space operation on $V$. The
definition does not depend on the basis of $V$ in which $P'$ is read: a change
of basis acts on the coordinates of $P'(s)$, and hence on those of
$\dot P(s)$, by the same constant invertible linear map, which commutes with
multiplication by the scalar $1/\tau'(s)$. Since $P'$ and $1/\tau'$ are
continuous, $\dot P$ is continuous; equivalently, the proper-time derivative of
a $C^1$ field is a continuous field.

**The proper-time reading.** Since $\tau$ is a strictly increasing bijection
$I\to J$ with inverse $\rho$, one has $\rho(\tau(s))=s$ and therefore
$(P\circ\rho)\circ\tau=P$ on $I$. Fix $s\in I$; the components of $P$ in a
basis of $V$ are differentiable at $s$ and $\rho$ is differentiable at
$\tau(s)$, so the scalar chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]) applied to each
component of $P\circ\rho$ gives

$$P'(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s))\,\tau'(s), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \dot P(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s)) .$$

At an endpoint of $I$ this is the one-sided reading of the derivative, as in
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. Thus $\dot P$ is exactly the
derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter of the field $P$ read
along the parametrisation $s\mapsto\tau(s)$; for every $u\in J$ the chain rule
on $J$ gives $(P\circ\rho)'(u)=P'(\rho(u))\rho'(u)=\dot P(\rho(u))$.

**(b) The four-force notation.** Let $m>0$ be constant and suppose the
four-velocity $U:I\to V$ of $x$ is $C^1$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]); by that definition $U$ is
always continuous, and $U$ is $C^1$ whenever the worldline $x$ is $C^2$. Then
$P:=mU$ is a $C^1$ map $I\to V$ and $F:=\dot P$ is called the **four-force**
on the particle. In an inertial frame the components of $F$ are the
derivatives of the components of the four-momentum with respect to the
proper-time parameter: writing $P^a(u)$ for the components of $P$ as a
function of the proper-time parameter $u=\tau(s)$, one has
$F^a(s)=\frac{d}{du}P^a(u)\big|_{u=\tau(s)}$.

**(c) Scope.** This item introduces a derivative and a name only. It asserts no
force law, no field equation, no equation of motion and no existence or
uniqueness of solutions of any equation of motion; in particular the
hypothesis that $U$ be $C^1$ is a regularity hypothesis on the given
worldline, not a dynamical statement. The identities satisfied by $F$ for a
stipulated four-momentum field are proved in
[[lem-sr-four-force-and-work-energy-identities]], and a physical force law
requires the separate model premise [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]].
The names four-momentum and four-force, and the units in which the components
of $P$ and $F$ are measured, belong to the framework's coordinate and unit
conventions ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]); the
mathematical content asserted here is the derivative construction (a) and the
notation (b) alone. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the dimensionless four-velocity lies on the future unit
hyperboloid $\{v \in C^{+}:\eta(v,v)=-1\}$.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = (0,w)$ in the frame coordinates, identified with $w$ via the spatial basis.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau(s) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(u),x'(u))}\,du$ for a base point
$s_0 \in I$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]). Then:

**(i)** $\tau$ is differentiable at every $s \in I$, with one-sided derivatives
at the endpoints of $I$, and

$$\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)} > 0$$

for every $s \in I$; since $\tau'$ is this composition of continuous maps,
$\tau$ is $C^{1}$ on $I$.

**(ii)** $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$, hence injective, and its image
$J := \tau[I]$ is an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with at least two
elements, so $\tau : I \to J$ is a bijection.

**(iii)** The inverse $\rho : J \to I$ of $\tau$ is continuous and strictly
increasing, and it is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of $J$ with

$$\rho'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{1}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} > 0 ;$$

hence $\rho$ is $C^{1}$ on $J$.

**(iv)** The reparametrized curve $y := x \circ \rho : J \to A$ is a $C^{1}$
future timelike worldline whose tangent at the proper-time parameter $\tau(s)$ is

$$(x \circ \rho)'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

in particular $y$ is parametrized by its own proper time up to the additive
constant of the base point.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with stationary observer $n:=e_0$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); let $E_n,q_n$ be the observer
quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].

**(a)** For every $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the coordinate components of $P$ in
the frame are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,\,q^1,q^2,q^3)$, where
$q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3q^ie_i$; if $P$ is future timelike then
$E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\sum_{i=1}^3(q^i)^2$ with $E=E_n(P)$.

**(b)** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) whose chart coordinate path is
$t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w:=r'$ and
$\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]],
[[def-rational-power]]); then $|w|<c$, the four-velocity is
$U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(e),
and for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant the components are $P=m\gamma_w(c,w)$, that
is $E_n(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3m\gamma_ww^ie_i$.

**(c)** Let $B(\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] with
parameter $\beta=(v/c)s$, where $v\in\mathbb R$, $|v|<c$, and
$s\in\mathbb R^3$ is a unit spatial coordinate vector ($s\cdot s=1$), and let $P'$
denote the components of the same vector $P$ after the coordinate change
$x'=B(\beta)x$, with $B(\beta)$ here denoting its frame matrix. Put
$\gamma_v:=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbf p:=(P^1,P^2,P^3)$,
$p_\parallel:=s\cdot\mathbf p$, $\mathbf p_\parallel:=p_\parallel s$ and
$\mathbf p_\perp:=\mathbf p-p_\parallel s$, with the same projections
defining the primed components. Then

$$P'^0=\gamma_v\bigl(P^0-(v/c)\,p_\parallel\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\parallel=\gamma_v\bigl(\mathbf p_\parallel-(v/c)P^0s\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp,$$

equivalently $E'=\gamma_v(E-v\,p_\parallel)$,
$p'_\parallel=\gamma_v(p_\parallel-vE/c^2)$, $\mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp$. The quadratic
combination is invariant,
$E'^2-c^2|\mathbf p'|^2=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m(P)^2c^4$ for future timelike
$P$, while for future null $P$ one has $E=c|\mathbf p|$ and
$E'=c|\mathbf p'|$ in both coordinate systems; in particular the invariant
mass is frame-independent.

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $c>0$, and $n\in V$ is future unit
timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$ for the rest space of $n$,
$h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ for the rest
projection and $|w|:=\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ for the norm on $n^\perp$
([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)); recall from that
clause that $h$ is linear with image $n^\perp$ and kernel $\mathrm{span}(n)$,
that $V=\mathrm{span}(n)\oplus n^\perp$, and that the restriction of $\eta$ to
$n^\perp$ is positive definite.

**(a) Observer energy, spatial momentum and invariant mass.** For every $P$ in
the future closed cone $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ define

$$E_n(P):=-c\,\eta(P,n), \qquad q_n(P):=h(P),$$

and, when $P$ is nonzero future causal, define the **invariant mass** of $P$ by

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}}{c} .$$

Then $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$, $\eta(n,P)=-E_n(P)/c$, and

$$P=\frac{E_n(P)}{c}\,n+q_n(P)$$

is the unique decomposition of $P$ as a real multiple of $n$ plus a vector of
$n^\perp$: a vector $P$ has $P=\lambda n+w$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and
$w\in n^\perp$ if and only if $\lambda=E_n(P)/c$ and $w=q_n(P)$. Equivalently,
$E_n(P)$ and $q_n(P)$ are the unique pair consisting of a real number and a
vector of $n^\perp$ with that property. The pair $(E_n,q_n)$ is the
restriction to $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ of the pair of linear maps
$P\mapsto -c\,\eta(P,n)$ and $P\mapsto h(P)$ on $V$. For future null $P$ the
formula for $m(P)$ gives $m(P)=0$, because $\eta(P,P)=0$.

**(b) Rest-mass parameter, rest energy and kinetic energy.** Let $m>0$ and let
$P=mU$ with $U$ future timelike and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, the four-velocity
normalisation of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]. Then call $m$
the **rest-mass parameter** of $P$ as written, $mc^2$ its **rest energy**, and

$$T_n(P):=E_n(P)-mc^2$$

its **kinetic energy** relative to the observer $n$. Bilinearity gives
$\eta(P,P)=m^2\eta(U,U)=-m^2c^2$, so $m=m(P)>0$ is determined by $P$.
Thus $T_n(P)=E_n(P)-m(P)c^2$ is a function of $(P,n)$ on the future
timelike cone; recording $m$ supplies no independent parameter.

**(c) No positivity, inequality or measurement claim.** This definition claims
no positivity of $E_n$, no inequality or vanishing property of $T_n$, and no
physical measurement. The names observer energy, spatial momentum, invariant
mass, rest energy and kinetic energy, and the units joule, kilogram metre per
second and kilogram, belong to the unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and to the physical postulates
of this framework; the mathematical content asserted here is only the explicit
dependence of the five quantities on $P$, $n$ and $m$.

**(d) What the objects depend on.** $E_n$ and $q_n$ are functions of the pair
$(P,n)$: $q_n(P)$ is an element of the vector space $V$, not a coordinate
triple, and no basis of $V$ enters its definition, while

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.
If $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb Q$, then the real power $a^r=\exp(r\log a)$ agrees with the rational power of [[def-rational-power]]. For $r>0$, both conventions also give $0^r=0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the

   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last

**Everything is proved through

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],

[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all

field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All five objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with coordinates $x_1,x_2,x_3$, partial derivatives $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x_j$, Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\lvert\cdot\rvert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), divergence and curl as in [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and cross product as in [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Put

$$Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2,\qquad \delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad (\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}.$$

Then $Q$ is a $C^1$ tensor field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}Q=F\,\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F .$$

**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ (b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

The particle's own field is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no self-force. (ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed current alone. (iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within electromagnetism.

Both are $C^1$ on the open $\Omega$, and [F4] applied to $F=E$ and to $F=B$ gives $\operatorname{div}Q^{(E)}=E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\operatorname{div}Q^{(B)}=B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B$; since $\sigma=\varepsilon_0Q^{(E)}+\mu_0^{-1}Q^{(B)}$ and $\operatorname{div}$ is linear in its argument, $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\varepsilon_0(E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E)+\mu_0^{-1}(B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B)$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$.

Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]], the source fields $\rho,J$ are continuous
of [[def-em-sources]], the constants are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]],
the force density is
$f:=\rho E+J\times B$ of that clause (ii), in
$\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $g,\sigma,\Pi=-\sigma$ are the momentum
density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$, componentwise,

$$\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f,$$

that is, $\partial_tg_i-\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}=-(\rho E_i+(J\times B)_i)$ for every $i$, with $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed position and $\operatorname{div}$ taken at fixed time.

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Then for
every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and every $i$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{3}\sigma_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{3}\Pi_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx,$$

the closed-surface integrals being the finite face sums of that divergence
theorem.

(c) [Scope] The identities are conditional on the two adopted postulates. The
force density $f$ is defined only for the matter model of clause (ii), so no
claim is made about a prescribed current without such a matter model. No
conservation of field-plus-matter momentum follows without explicit matter
balances and their boundary fluxes. The field-momentum rate in (b) is the
boundary traction minus the integrated matter force; these terms can cancel,
and neither may be discarded without justification. The weak branch, singular sources and
non-integrable products are excluded as in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; no self-force, radiation reaction or
magnetic-monopole coupling is included, in accordance with the exclusions of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]. This is not an empirical claim.

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]] and satisfy, with the continuous source
fields $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]] and the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and
$\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]
applied at fixed times and $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed
position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Let $u$ and $S$ be
the energy density and Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E,$$

where $\operatorname{div}S$ is taken at fixed time and $J\cdot E$ is the
Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal
of $\partial\Omega'$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which
that divergence theorem is stated. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS,$$

the closed-surface integral being the finite face sum of that divergence
theorem and the derivative being the derivative of the one-variable function
$t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx$ on $(t_0,t_1)$.

(c) [Interpretation and scope] Under clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], $J\cdot E$ is the power density supplied to the
matter model of that coupling, so (a) and (b) read as a local, respectively
fixed-volume, energy balance of the field and that matter model. Nothing is
claimed for a prescribed current without such a matter model, for the weak
branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular sources, or at field points
where the products defining $u$ or $S$ are not locally integrable; the
fixed-volume identity retains both the work term and the boundary flux. The
field-energy rate can vanish by cancellation of these two terms; vanishing
boundary flux alone does not eliminate exchange with matter. A conservation
claim for field plus matter additionally requires an explicit matter balance. This is a
conditional consequence of the adopted postulates, not an empirical claim.
